opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly the term gets used pretty loosely these days, so I think it's worth being precise about it.

The way I think about it, a world model is a model that can simulate how an environment evolves over time, and crucially, how it responds to actions. A video model generates a plausible sequence of frames, which is already impressive, but it's passive. You give it a prompt and it plays out a clip. A world model has to answer a different question: given the current state of the world, and given that I, or an agent, do *this*, what happens next? So interactivity, or action-conditioning, is a big part of the definition for me.

The second ingredient is consistency over time. If you walk away from something and come back, it should still be there. If you knock something over, it should stay knocked over. That kind of persistence and memory is really hard, because the model isn't running a physics engine or a game engine with explicit state. It's learning all of this implicitly from data. So the degree to which a model maintains a coherent world, rather than just producing locally plausible frames, is a good test of how much of a world model it really is.

And third, I'd say there's an element of capturing the underlying dynamics, things like physics, cause and effect, how objects and agents behave, in a way that generalizes. You want to be able to drop into situations the model hasn't seen exactly and still get sensible behavior.

So it's less of a binary and more of a spectrum. Video generation models already have a lot of implicit world knowledge in them. That's partly why they're so interesting. But as you add real-time interaction, controllability, and long-horizon consistency, you move further along that spectrum toward something you'd call a true world model. And that's where it gets exciting, because then you can use it not just for content creation, but for things like training agents, robotics, and exploring environments that don't exist yet.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts passive video generation with interactive world models, but does not identify the visual focus of current world models as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It says video models contain implicit world knowledge, but does not suggest that generating realistic images or videos requires an internal representation of world behavior.

r003.rationale: It does not state that a world model need not generate pixels.

r004.rationale: It describes a world model as answering what happens next given the current state and an action.

r005.rationale: It does not attribute the prominence of visual world models to diffusion models’ success in visual generation.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's one we debated a lot internally, because the term gets used pretty loosely these days. For me, the core of it is this: a world model is a model that takes in actions and produces the consequences of those actions in a consistent environment, in real time, or at least interactively.

So if you contrast that with, say, a video generation model, a video model takes a prompt and generates a clip. It's an open-loop thing. You give it the text, and maybe an image, and it produces something, and that's it. A world model, the way we think about it, is closed-loop. There's an agent, whether that's a person or a policy, that's taking actions, and the model has to respond to those actions frame by frame, and it has to keep the world consistent as it does that. If I turn left and then turn right, the thing I saw before should still be there. If I pick something up, it should stay picked up. That memory and consistency piece is a big part of what separates a world model from something that just generates plausible-looking video.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that it needs to be interactive at a meaningful rate. If you can only get a frame every few seconds, you're not really simulating a world, you're generating a slideshow. So latency and the ability to respond in something close to real time is almost definitional for us.

And then the third piece, which I think is maybe the most interesting one from a research standpoint, is that the model has to have learned some notion of the dynamics of the world, not just the appearance of it. It has to understand that objects have physics, that characters move in certain ways, that cause leads to effect. And ideally that's learned from data rather than hand-coded, because the whole promise here is that you can build a simulator for anything, including things that would be very hard to write a traditional game engine or physics engine for.

So, to summarize: actions in, consequences out, in a consistent environment, in real time, with learned dynamics. That's roughly the bar we hold ourselves to when we say "world model."

r001.rationale: The response contrasts world models with open-loop video generation, but does not identify visual focus in current world models as a limitation.

r002.rationale: It says world models should learn dynamics rather than only appearance, but does not connect an internal representation of world behavior to generating realistic images or video.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that a world model can operate without generating pixels.

r004.rationale: It says a world model takes actions as input and produces their consequences, responding frame by frame in a consistent environment.

r005.rationale: The response does not attribute the prominence of visual world models to diffusion models.

astra-6.text:
I think of a world model as a model that captures how an environment works—not just what it looks like at a particular moment, but how it changes over time and how actions affect it. If I take some action, can the model predict what might happen next?

That doesn’t necessarily mean modeling the entire physical world. The environment could be a game or some much more constrained setting. The important question is what the model understands well enough to let you reason about possible futures. Can you use it to explore alternatives and make decisions?

And I think that’s a spectrum. A model can capture some aspects of the world very well and fail on others. So I’d ask less whether something qualifies as a world model in an absolute sense, and more what it models, how reliably, and for what purpose.

r001.rationale: It contrasts modeling behavior with describing how an environment looks, but does not identify visual focus as a limitation of current world models.

r002.rationale: It does not connect realistic image or video generation to an internal representation of world behavior.

r003.rationale: It says a model need not represent the entire physical world, but does not state that a world model need not generate pixels.

r004.rationale: It says a model should predict what might happen next after an action in an environment.

r005.rationale: It does not mention diffusion models or explain the prominence of visual world models.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of a world model as a model that captures how some part of the world behaves. Given a situation, and perhaps an action, it can predict what might happen next. That doesn’t necessarily mean modeling the entire physical world. It could be a much narrower environment.

The interesting question is whether it has learned something that generalizes beyond the examples it has seen. Can it handle a new situation while preserving the relevant relationships and constraints? And can you use it to reason about alternatives—if I do this instead of that, how does the outcome change?

So I’d think of it as a spectrum, rather than a binary label. A model can capture some aspects of the world very well and have a very incomplete understanding of others.
